newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Chinese U.N. dragon breathes fire over Taiwan.
newsitem.headline: Chinese U.N. dragon breathes fire over Taiwan.

text.p: China, often considered a slumbering dragon at the United Nations, has suddenly breathed fire by casting its first Security Council veto in nearly a quarter of a century to block the dispatch of U.N. peacekeepers to Guatemala.
The 14 other council members all supported the resolution to dispatch 155 military observers to monitor an accord ending 30 years of civil war.
The peacekeepers were not the issue, as far as China was concerned, but the fact that Guatemala has close ties with Taiwan and refuses to show signs of contrition.

Not only does Guatemala recognize Taiwan, but each year since 1993 it has joined with a number of other small countries to sponsor a General Assembly resolution aimed at securing U.N. membership for the Asian economic powerhouse.
To make matters worse, in China's eyes, Guatemala invited Taiwan's foreign minister to the Dec. 29 peace signing ceremony in Guatemala City.

And, shortly before the Security Council meeting got under way, the Guatemalan foreign minister wrote a letter to the council president which further irked China by referring to Taiwan as a government, diplomats said.
Taiwan was expelled from the United Nations in 1971 and replaced by Beijing as the rightful representative of China.

China regards Taiwan as a renegade province that will one day be reunited with the motherland. Any moves to support it or recognize it as an independent entity are guaranteed to drive Beijing to distraction.
Since taking its U.N. seat, it has exercised its veto on only two previous occasions.

Once, in August 1972, was to block U.N. membership for Bangladesh after it seceded from Pakistan, China's friend. The second veto was cast less than a month later, together with Russia, to kill an amendment to a Middle East resolution.

Russia has wielded a veto 116 times since the birth of the United Nations in 1945, while the United States has used it on 70 occasions. Britain's tally is 30 vetoes and France's 18. The Nationalist Chinese cast a single veto, in 1955, to prevent Mongolia from joining the United Nations.

Coincidentally, China's U.N. envoy, Qin Huasun, cast his country's first veto in nearly 25 years while Ambassador Hisashi Owada of Japan, Beijing's historic adversary, was presiding over the 15-nation council for the first time.

China usually adopts a low-key approach at the United Nations where, despite its big power status, it prefers a role as champion of third world nations. But In recent years, it has abstained on a number of council resolutions, including some prompted by Iraq's invasion of Kuwait.
Beijing takes a dim view of sanctions and anything it construes as interference in a country's internal afffairs. This is widely interpreted as a warning never to attempt such liberties with China.

But China raised its profile last February when, in circumstances similar to the dispute over Guatemala, it balked at renewing a U.N. peacekeeping force in Haiti -- also because of that country's ties with Taiwan.

After holding the Haiti operation hostage for several days, China finally relented and voted for a scaled-down compromise. A Chinese diplomatic delegation visited Haiti last July for the first time in 40 years.
On Guatemala, it remained uncertain until just before the council met whether China would use its veto or pull back from the brink and be satisfied to abstain.

Its U.N. spokesmen, Chen Ranfeng, repeatedly stressed that respect for China's sovereignty and territorial integrity was at stake and that the issue could be resolved if only Guatemala made the appropriate gestures.

China never spelled out publicly what Guatemala was expected to do. But diplomats said it sought a pledge to refrain from sponsoring further pro-Taiwan U.N. resolutions and to stop receiving high-ranking Taiwanese visitors.
